title.en: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
title.vi: Ở Bosnia và Herzegovina, trẻ em hội chứng Down đang sử dụng trò chơi điện tử để lướt web an toàn hơn bằng SafeClick (*SafeClick*) bảo vệ quyền riêng tư kỹ thuật số (*digital safety*). Trẻ em được hỗ trợ qua trò chơi giúp tránh khỏi sự cô lập kỹ thuật số (*digital isolation*). Trò chơi điện tử đóng vai trò như chiếc la bàn giúp trẻ tự tin khám phá Internet mà không sợ lạc lối. Bạn hãy cùng tìm hiểu cách trò chơi này mang lại thay đổi tích cực cho cộng đồng. Các nhà phát triển đã tạo ra trợ lý ảo cú Sol (*Sol the Owl*) để đồng hành cùng các em. Hãy thử tìm hiểu thêm về cách ứng dụng này hỗ trợ người khuyết tật trí tuệ (*intellectual disabilities*) trong thời đại số hóa hiện nay nhé.

hook.en: SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission.

sections.body_en: *This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.*

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI. To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.

Stefan Filipovic. Photo used with permission.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

**Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.**

**Stefan Filipovic (SF):** We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes. We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.

The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.

The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.

**GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?**

**SF:** While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them. Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations. We wanted to try something different.

With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.
